0.value:
Gives the dot product of two vectors: multiply them element by element and add up - one number that says how much they point the same way.

For two vectors of length 1 the dot product is the cosine of the angle between them: 1 when they point the same way, 0 at right angles, -1 when opposite. For longer vectors it is scaled by both lengths. With one of them a unit direction, it is the PROJECTION: how far the other reaches along that direction - the component of a movement along an axis, of a force along a surface, of a pose along a learned direction.

Reach for it to compare directions (similarity), to project onto an axis, or to test for right angles (dot 0).

FOR ARRAYS OF MORE THAN ONE DIMENSION:
2-D with 2-D is matrix multiplication, the same as np.matmul. A set of vectors (N rows of 3) with one vector of 3 gives N dot products - every row against the same direction at once.

SYNTAX:
np.dot
(no arguments)

INPUTS and PARAMETERS:

in 1:
The first vector (a list is turned into an array). Receiving it calculates and sends.

in 2:
The second vector. It is only stored, so it must arrive BEFORE in 1;
nothing is sent until it has. The lengths must match (for 2-D, the columns of in 1 must match the rows of in 2), or an error is printed and nothing is sent.

OUTPUTS:

dot product:
A float for two vectors; an array for the larger cases.

READING THE DEMO:
Two pads, one per vector, and both draw the whole picture. Drag the yellow dot on the left pad: it is the tip of a (yellow arrow), sent as [x, y] to in 1. Drag the blue dot on the right pad to turn b (blue arrow): its position is divided by its own length (np.linalg.norm), so b always has length 1 and only its direction counts; it goes to in 2. The magenta arrow is b times the dot product - the shadow a casts on b, with the grey line dropping from a's tip onto it. Its length is the answer: a long shadow when a points along b, none at right angles, and it flips behind the origin, negative, when a points away. With a of length 1 the answer is the cosine of the angle between them.

'b' goes through 't bang array': the array is stored in in 2 first, then the bang makes a re-send, so moving either dot updates the answer. 't bang float' sets the dot product as the operand of '*', then bangs b through it. The pads save where their dots are; load_bang bangs each pad's vectors inlet, which sends that position, to start the picture.

RELATED:
np.inner is the same for vectors but pairs rows with rows for 2-D arrays. np.matmul is the matrix product. np.linalg.norm gives a length (the square root of a vector dotted with itself). np.cross gives the vector at right angles to both. t.cosine_similarity gives the cosine directly, whatever the lengths.
